meta.name: GI Bleed — Hemorrhagic Shock from Upper GI Hemorrhage

patient.name: Walter Higgins
patient.chiefComplaint: Vomiting blood, feeling weak and dizzy

history.hpi: Patient reports several episodes of vomiting bright red blood mixed with dark, coffee-ground material over the past two hours, along with black, tarry stools since yesterday. Reports progressive weakness, dizziness when standing, and lightheadedness. Denies abdominal trauma, denies chest pain.
medications: Ibuprofen 400 mg PO as needed for joint pain (daily use over past 2 weeks)
history.lastOralIntake: Dry toast, several hours prior to arrival; vomited most of it with blood
history.events: Wife called 911 after witnessing him vomit a large amount of blood in the bathroom and appear pale and unsteady

scene.dispatch: 68-year-old male, vomiting, possible GI bleeding, residence
scene.location: Single-family home, upstairs bathroom, patient found seated on the floor next to the toilet
scene.safety: No hazards to crew; visible blood in and around the toilet bowl
scene.bystanders: Wife present, witnessed the vomiting episode and called 911 immediately
visualCues: Bright red blood with dark coffee-ground material in the toilet bowl
Patient pale and diaphoretic, leaning against the bathtub
Empty ibuprofen bottle on the bathroom counter
Patient appears weak, has difficulty sitting upright unassisted

phases.name: Initial Contact
phases.description: Crew arrives to find a 68-year-old male seated on the bathroom floor, pale and diaphoretic, with visible hematemesis in the toilet. He reports black tarry stools since yesterday and progressive weakness.

clinicalPresentation.airway: Patent, speaking in full sentences but with a weak voice
clinicalPresentation.circulation: Radial pulses weak and rapid, skin pale and diaphoretic, capillary refill delayed ~3 seconds
otherFindings: Visible hematemesis in the toilet bowl with coffee-ground appearance
Reports black, tarry stools since yesterday
clinicalPresentation.patientSpeech: "I feel so weak... I think I threw up blood."

transitions.if: IV access and fluid bolus started
transitions.condition: Crew recognizes signs of hypovolemic shock from suspected upper GI hemorrhage and establishes vascular access, checks blood glucose, applies cardiac monitoring, and begins fluid resuscitation.

phases.name: IV access and fluid bolus started
phases.description: Crew establishes IV access, obtains a blood glucose and full vital signs, applies cardiac monitoring, and begins rapid isotonic fluid resuscitation targeting a MAP of 65 mmHg for suspected hemorrhagic shock.
phases.triggerCondition: After recognizing pallor, diaphoresis, tachycardia, and hypotension consistent with hemorrhagic shock from the reported hematemesis and melena, the crew establishes IV access, obtains a blood glucose and full vital signs, and begins a rapid isotonic fluid bolus.

clinicalPresentation.circulation: 18-gauge IV established in the AC, fluid bolus infusing, radial pulses still weak
clinicalPresentation.patientSpeech: "Is that helping? I still feel dizzy."

expectedActions.shortAction: Establish IV access (18-gauge preferred); place IO if unsuccessful within 2 attempts/90 sec
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Establish IV access. If unable to obtain within two attempts or less than 90 seconds, place an IO needle
expectedActions.rationale: Vascular access is required for fluid resuscitation in hemorrhagic shock.

expectedActions.shortAction: Check blood glucose; correct if less than 60 mg/dL
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Check blood sugar, and correct if less than 60 mg/dL
expectedActions.rationale: Altered mentation in shock can be compounded by hypoglycemia and should be ruled out.

expectedActions.shortAction: Apply cardiac monitor and pulse oximetry; obtain EtCO2
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Cardiac monitor. Pulse oximetry and EtCO2 (reading of less than 25 mmHg may be sign of poor perfusion)
expectedActions.rationale: Continuous monitoring detects deterioration in perfusion status.

expectedActions.shortAction: Give 500 mL isotonic fluid bolus, pressure-infused, targeting MAP 65 mmHg
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: IV fluid volume goal attained by giving boluses that are pressure infused over less than 15 minutes each... Physiologic target: MAP goal 65 mmHg. Fluid goal of up to 30 mL/kg of isotonic fluid by administering rapid, predetermined boluses (e.g., 500 mL) unless the MAP goal is achieved, or pulmonary edema develops.
expectedActions.rationale: Rapid fluid resuscitation is the primary treatment for hemorrhagic shock in the field.

expectedActions.shortAction: Identify hematemesis and melena as the bleeding source driving hypovolemic shock
expectedActions.rationale: Correctly identifying the hemorrhage source informs destination and hospital notification.

transitions.condition: After one to two fluid boluses, blood pressure trends upward toward the MAP goal, heart rate begins to slow, and mental status remains intact; crew prepares for rapid transport with advance hospital notification.
IV access is delayed, boluses are not repeated, or the crew underestimates ongoing blood loss, allowing hypotension and tachycardia to worsen toward decompensated hemorrhagic shock.

phases.name: MAP improves, perfusion stabilizes
phases.description: Blood pressure trends upward following fluid resuscitation, heart rate begins to slow, and the patient remains alert. Crew provides advance notification to the receiving facility and prepares for transport with ongoing reassessment.
phases.triggerCondition: After one to two fluid boluses, blood pressure trends upward toward the MAP goal, heart rate begins to slow, and mental status remains intact.

clinicalPresentation.circulation: Radial pulses stronger, capillary refill improving to under 2 seconds
otherFindings: Advance notification given to receiving facility for suspected active GI hemorrhage

expectedActions.shortAction: Provide advance notification to receiving facility for suspected active GI hemorrhage
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Provide advanced notification to the hospital
expectedActions.rationale: Advance notification allows the receiving facility to prepare blood products and endoscopy resources.

expectedActions.shortAction: Reassess vital signs and response to fluid therapy throughout transport
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Reassess vital signs and response to therapeutic interventions throughout transport
expectedActions.rationale: Ongoing hemorrhage can recur; continuous reassessment detects re-deterioration early.

phases.name: Fluid resuscitation delayed or inadequate
phases.description: IV access is delayed or fluid boluses are not repeated despite persistent hypotension, allowing ongoing occult hemorrhage to progress toward decompensated shock with worsening mentation and vital signs.
phases.triggerCondition: IV access is delayed or the crew fails to repeat fluid boluses despite persistent hypotension, allowing ongoing blood loss to progress toward decompensated shock.

clinicalPresentation.airway: Patent, slurred and slow to respond
clinicalPresentation.circulation: Thready, rapid pulses; skin pale, cool, and mottled
clinicalPresentation.motorFunction: Generalized weakness, slow to respond to questions
otherFindings: Repeat blood pressure significantly lower than initial
clinicalPresentation.patientSpeech: "...I don't... feel right..." (slurred, slow to respond)

expectedActions.shortAction: Recognize decompensated hemorrhagic shock; give repeat fluid bolus and expedite transport
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Hypotension indicates uncompensated shock, which may progress to cardiopulmonary failure within minutes.
expectedActions.rationale: Delayed recognition of ongoing hemorrhage risks rapid progression to cardiopulmonary collapse.
